summary: To ensure baseline interoperability, WebRTC endpoints must support a minimum set of audio codecs. This informational RFC gives guidelines on other suitable codecs worth offering, to avoid transcoding when setting up sessions.

plainLanguage.summary: WebRTC calls between browsers already work well. Calls between a browser and an older phone or cordless handset do not, because those devices use different audio codecs and the network has to convert the sound. This document lists the extra codecs a WebRTC endpoint should offer so those calls can start without any conversion.

questions: how to avoid transcoding in webrtc
subtitle: Which extra audio codecs a WebRTC endpoint should offer so calls to older phones connect without transcoding.

tldr.problem: WebRTC endpoints all support Opus, so calls between them work. But many calls go to handsets, fixed VoIP phones and cordless devices that do not, and those calls fall back to a narrowband codec or are transcoded in a gateway.
tldr.mechanism: The document recommends that endpoints offer AMR-WB, AMR and G.722 as well, each with its own payload format, so that a call to a device which speaks one of them can start with the same codec on both sides.
tldr.outcome: Callers avoid the quality loss, the added delay and the gateway cost that transcoding brings, and the list stays open to other codecs once a use case for them is identified.

today: RFC 7875 is an Informational document published in May 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it is guidance rather than a specification: the mandatory codec requirements it builds on are in RFC 7874.

sections.title: Why Offer More Codecs
sections.content:
It has been anticipated that WebRTC will not remain an isolated island, and that some WebRTC endpoints will need to communicate with devices used in other existing networks with the help of a gateway. To maximize the possibility of establishing the session without the need for audio transcoding, RFC 7874 recommends including in the offer other suitable audio codecs beyond those that are mandatory to implement.

The mandatory implementation of Opus can guarantee codec interoperability, without transcoding, at a voice quality better than narrowband PSTN quality between WebRTC endpoints. WebRTC is also expected to be used to communicate with other kinds of endpoints, for instance as an access technology to VoLTE services, or to interoperate with fixed or mobile circuit-switched or VoIP services such as mobile circuit-switched voice over 3GPP 2G and 3G networks, or DECT-based VoIP telephony.

A significant number of calls are therefore likely to occur between terminals supporting WebRTC and other terminals, such as mobile handsets, fixed VoIP terminals and DECT terminals, that support neither WebRTC nor Opus. Those calls are likely to be either of low narrowband PSTN quality using G.711 at both ends, or affected by transcoding operations.

The document's terms are worth noting. Legacy networks mean the conversational networks that are already deployed, such as the PSTN, the PLMN, and the IP/IMS networks offering VoIP services, including the 3GPP 4G Evolved Packet System supporting voice over LTE. A WebRTC endpoint can be a browser or a non-browser, also called a WebRTC device or WebRTC native application.

The codecs considered here are recommended only for WebRTC endpoints for which interoperability with other non-WebRTC endpoints and non-WebRTC-based services is relevant. Other use cases may justify offering other additional codecs to avoid transcoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Every WebRTC endpoint speaks Opus, so two of them always connect. The problem is the call to a device that does not speak Opus, such as an old handset or a cordless phone. If both ends cannot use the same codec, the network has to convert the sound from one format to another, and that costs quality and time.

sections.title: What Transcoding Costs
sections.content:
The document lists three drawbacks of transcoding.

Voice quality is significantly degraded by transcoding. For instance, the degradation is around 0.2 to 0.3 MOS, the Mean Opinion Score defined in ITU-T Recommendation P.800, for most transcoding use cases with the AMR-WB codec at 12.65 kbit/s, and in the same range for other wideband transcoding cases. If G.711 is used as a fallback codec for interoperation, wideband voice quality is lost, and the reduction down to narrow band clearly degrades the quality of service that users perceive, leading to shorter and less frequent calls. If transcoding is performed between Opus and another wideband codec, wideband communication could be maintained but with degraded quality: the MOS values for transcoding between AMR-WB at 12.65 kbit/s and Opus at 16 kbit/s in both directions are significantly lower than those of AMR-WB at 12.65 kbit/s or Opus at 16 kbit/s on their own. In degraded conditions, adding defects such as audio artifacts due to packet losses and audio effects due to the cascading of different packet loss recovery algorithms may result in a quality below the acceptable limit for customers.

Conversational interactivity is degraded, because transcoding increases the end-to-end latency in both directions. Transcoding requires full de-packetization for decoding of the media stream, including de-jitter buffering and packet loss recovery, then re-encoding, re-packetization and resending. The delays produced by all these operations are additive and may increase the end-to-end delay up to 1 second, much beyond the acceptable limit.

Transcoding also places important additional cost on network gateways, mainly related to codec implementation, codec licences, deployment, and testing and validation. Transcoding of wideband to wideband would require more CPU processing and be more costly than transcoding between narrowband codecs.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting the sound costs three things. Callers hear worse quality, typically about a quarter of a point on the mean opinion score scale. Each side waits longer, because the audio has to be unpacked, decoded, re-encoded and repacked, which together can add up to a second. And the operator of the gateway pays for codec licences and processing time.

sections.title: AMR-WB and AMR for Mobile Networks
sections.content:
The Adaptive Multi-Rate WideBand (AMR-WB) is a 3GPP-defined speech codec that is mandatory to implement in any 3GPP terminal supporting wideband speech communication. It is used in circuit-switched mobile telephony services and in new multimedia telephony services over IP/IMS, and it is used for voice over LTE as specified by GSMA. AMR is a 3GPP-defined speech codec that is mandatory to implement in any 3GPP terminal that supports voice communication, which covers mobile phone calls using GSM and 3G cellular systems as well as multimedia telephony services over IP/IMS and 4G/VoLTE.

The use case for AMR-WB is that the market of personal voice communication is driven by mobile terminals, and AMR-WB is now very widely implemented in devices and networks offering HD voice. A high number of calls are likely to occur between WebRTC endpoints and mobile 3GPP terminals offering AMR-WB, so the use of AMR-WB by WebRTC endpoints would allow transcoding-free interoperation with all mobile 3GPP wideband terminals. WebRTC endpoints running on mobile terminals may also reuse the AMR-WB codec already implemented on those devices.

For AMR, although more and more terminal devices are HD voice and support AMR-WB, there are still a high number of legacy terminals supporting only AMR, with no wideband capabilities, still in use. A user of a WebRTC endpoint on a device with an AMR module wants to reach another user who can only be reached on a mobile device that supports only AMR, and the use of AMR by WebRTC endpoints would allow transcoding-free interoperation with all mobile 3GPP terminals.

The guidelines are the same in shape for both codecs. The payload format is described in RFC 4867, with a bandwidth-efficient format and one speech frame encapsulated in each RTP packet. To ensure interoperability with 4G/VoLTE, the more specific IMS profile for voice derived from the 3GPP media handling specification should be considered. A WebRTC endpoint offering AMR-WB should also offer AMR, with AMR-WB listed first as the preferred payload type with respect to the other narrowband codecs, and with a bandwidth-efficient payload format preferred. It should be capable of operating AMR-WB with any subset of the nine codec modes and source-controlled rate operation, and offer at least one AMR-WB configuration with parameter settings as defined in Table 6.1 of the 3GPP media handling specification. For AMR, the endpoint should be capable of operating with any subset of the eight codec modes and source-controlled rate operation, and offer at least one configuration with parameter settings as defined in Tables 6.1 and 6.2 of the same specification. In both cases the offer should not restrict the codec modes offered, and restrictions on the use of codec modes may be included in the answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The two mobile codecs are the ones already inside 3GPP handsets, so a WebRTC endpoint that supports them can talk to any mobile phone without converting the audio. AMR-WB is the wideband one used for HD voice. AMR is the older narrowband one that a lot of phones still have. An endpoint should offer both, with AMR-WB first.

sections.title: G.722 for Cordless and Fixed Phones
sections.content:
G.722 is an ITU-T-defined wideband speech codec, approved by the ITU-T in 1988. It is a royalty-free codec that is common in a wide range of terminals and endpoints supporting wideband speech and requiring low complexity. The complexity of G.722 is estimated to 10 MIPS, which is 2.5 to 3 times lower than AMR-WB.

G.722 has been chosen by ETSI DECT as the mandatory wideband codec for New Generation DECT, in order to greatly increase the voice quality by extending the bandwidth from narrowband to wideband. It is the wideband codec required for terminals certified as CAT-iq DECT, and version 2.0 of the CAT-iq specifications has been approved by GSMA as the minimum requirements for the HD voice logo on fixed devices, that is, broadband connections using the G.722 codec.

The use case is that DECT cordless phones are still widely used to offer short-range wireless connection to PSTN or VoIP services. G.722 has also been specified by ETSI as the mandatory wideband codec for IMS multimedia telephony communication service and supplementary services using fixed broadband access. Supporting G.722 would allow transcoding-free IP interoperation between WebRTC endpoints and fixed VoIP terminals, including DECT CAT-iq terminals supporting G.722. WebRTC endpoints running on fixed terminals that implement G.722 may also reuse the codec already implemented on those devices.

The payload format for G.722 is defined in RFC 3551, with each octet of the stream of octets produced by the codec octet-aligned in an RTP packet. The sampling frequency for the G.722 codec is 16 kHz, but the RTP clock rate is set to 8000 Hz in SDP, to stay backward compatible with an erroneous definition in the original version of the RTP audio/video profile.
sections.plainLanguage: G.722 is the wideband codec used by cordless phones and by fixed broadband VoIP equipment. It is free of royalties and cheap to run, at around 10 MIPS, which is two and a half to three times less work than AMR-WB. An endpoint that supports it can call a cordless handset without converting the sound.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document points readers to RFC 7874, WebRTC Audio Codec and Processing Requirements, for the relevant security considerations. Implementers making use of the additional codecs considered here are advised to also refer more specifically to the Security Considerations sections of RFC 4867, for AMR and AMR-WB, and of RFC 3551, for the RTP audio/video profile. The document states no security considerations of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds no rules of its own. It points to the security sections of the specifications for WebRTC audio, for the AMR and AMR-WB payload formats, and for the RTP profile those formats run on.
